newsitem.title: FRANCE: Border-free Europe helps Mafia bosses - France.
newsitem.headline: Border-free Europe helps Mafia bosses - France.

text.p: France said on Tuesday that the dismantling of European Union borders had fostered the spread of organised crime, with Mafia barons investing dirty money and creating rearguard networks on its territory.

Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre, launching a week-long forum in Paris attended by 200 police chiefs from 80 countries, said some crime gangs had recently specialised in spiriting away humanitarian aid.

"The free movement of people and the growth of data transmission networks have fuelled the penetration into our territory of foreign criminals who invest or create networks of contacts," Debre said in his speech.

"So far, the Mafia phenomenon has not managed to take root (outside Italy) but the threat exists, especially in drug trafficking and money laundering," he told the conference organised by France's Institute for Higher Studies into Internal Security (IHESI).

Crime fighters have warned that the single market set up by the European Union in 1993, abolishing internal border controls, played into the hands of drug barons. Governments have replied that other checks would be set up to compensate for the loss.

Investigators report that Italian organised crime has in recent years set up bases in several European countries. In France, Italian gangs have laundered illicit profits by investing in hotels and tourism complexes on the Riviera.
Italian gangs, Colombian drug cartels and newcomers from formerly Communist East Europe have also forged new ties.

Calling for increased global cooperation to crack down on money laundering, Debre said organised crime was changing and tackling new activities -- "Embezzling humanitarian aid, defrauding European Union subsidies, selling nuclear technologies, and so on."
He said: "We are seeing more and more organisations which specialise in making relief aid evaporate."
In a denunciation rare for a French government minister, Debre said the tiny principality of Monaco was "often used as a rearguard base or a place of transit".

Investigators say they have long suspected that much of the cash in circulation in tax-free Monaco, which boasts tight banking secrecy, comes not from the takings of respectable millionaires but of drug barons.

Raymond Kendall, secretary-general of the France-based Interpol international police agency, called at the Paris forum for more international cooperation in pooling data on crime, even if this meant states giving up part of their sovereignty.

In a report on organised crime published as the conference started, IHESI president Marcel Leclerc wrote: "Organised crime knows no frontiers. Given the new scale of the threats it represents, it is an immediate danger which demands a response from democratic states."
